subject: Prompt affinity metering / billing boundary for cached hits

Subject: Prompt affinity metering — how do you treat warm/cached prefixes?

Hi Laura,

Thanks for the demo last week — the latency looked great. We're working through the pricing section of the RFP and I need one clear sentence we can show procurement: when you serve a cached prefix (a ‘warm’ prompt state), do you charge tokens for that prefix on the hosted API, or only for the tokens the model actually computes on the request?

A few concrete follow-ups that matter to us:
- Multi-session reuse: if a user’s conversation hits a cached prefix created by a previous session (same client but different session ID), do you still count it as a cache hit?
- Partial overlap: if the incoming prompt shares the first N tokens with a cached prefix but diverges mid-prompt, how do you split billing?
- Warm-up/prefetch: we often prefetch common prefixes (for faster cold-starts). Do those prefetch requests create billable events? Our security team also asked whether prefetch traffic is identifiable for discounting.

We need this to be explicit in the contract (or in a short appendix) so procurement can compare apples-to-apples. Can you share examples and a suggested clause?

Thanks,
Tom
Tom Briggs
Head of Platform Procurement
Orchid Health

Hi Tom,

Appreciate the clear questions — you’re asking exactly the right things for procurement. Below is a concise summary followed by three short examples we can drop into an appendix or contract addendum. Happy to hop on a quick call if you prefer to walk through the scenarios.

Short answer (one-liner for procurement):
- Redwood does not bill model compute for a prefix that is served 100% from our prefix/KV cache (exact-match, no model execution). For partial hits, we bill compute for the tokens that require model execution; request-level metadata and small I/O costs are not charged separately. Prefetch requests that intentionally prime the cache are considered regular API calls and are billable unless captured under an enterprise prefetch credit in your agreement.

Examples (feel free to paste into the RFP appendix):
1) Exact-match prefix hit
- Scenario: Session A generates Prompt P and creates cached state S. Later Session B requests exactly the same Prompt P (token-for-token).
- Billing: No model compute billed for the prefix P; customer is charged only for any new tokens produced by the model (if any).

2) Partial overlap (prefix matches N tokens, then diverges)
- Scenario: Cached state S contains tokens T1..T100. Incoming prompt shares T1..T60 then diverges.
- Billing: Tokens T1..T60 are served from cache (no compute billed). Tokens T61..T100 and onward are computed and billed per normal token pricing. We attribute billing to the request that triggered model execution.

3) Prefetch / warm-up requests
- Scenario: Client issues prefetch calls to populate cache (no user-facing request).
- Billing: Prefetch calls are treated as standard API requests and are billable. For enterprise customers we can include a prefetch-credit line in the SOW that exempts a negotiated % of prefetch volume from billing (example: 50% rebate on prefetch tokens up to a monthly cap).

Optional enterprise protections we commonly include:
- Cache-hit rebate: a negotiated rebate (percent or $) on billed usage attributed to cache misses vs hits, often used to adjust unit economics for high-reuse workloads.
- Logging proof: We provide logs that show prefix-match events and keys (hashed) for audit. We can expose a dashboard slice so your SREs can validate hit rates.

I attached a short spreadsheet with worked examples for reference (orchid_cache-billing-examples.xlsx) and our current rate card (Redwood_rate_card_v3.pdf). Ben (cc’d) will propose commercial language if you want an NDA-friendly clause for procurement.

Next steps:
1) I can draft two contract appendix options: (A) standard rate card language (no prefetch credits), (B) enterprise addendum (prefetch credits + cache-hit rebate + logging SLA).
2) If you share expected monthly token traffic and an example reuse pattern, we’ll run a proforma showing the economics of both options.

Would Friday morning work for a quick 30-min sync?

Best,

Thanks Laura — that level of detail helps. Two quick clarifications and an edge case:

1) Session affinity: we run a multi-tenant mobile app where the same end user can hit different app servers (different session IDs). Is cache matching keyed by client + session ID, or by hashed prompt content? In other words, how fragile is a cache hit to session identifiers?

2) Re: partial overlap: in your example you mention attributing billed tokens to the request that triggers model execution. For accounting purposes our procurement team wants to know whether you show both the cache-served token count and the computed token count on the invoice/audit report.

3) Edge-case: we sometimes inject per-request metadata (like locale or user_flags) that appears as an extra header token. If that extra token changes, but the core user prompt is identical, will the system still match the cached prefix?

If you can give a one-paragraph amendment we can show procurement that covers session affinity and per-request metadata, that would be ideal.

—Tom

Tom — thanks for the follow-ups. Below is a short amendment you can show procurement; I’ve kept the language non-technical and contract-friendly. I’ll attach the formal appendix if you want to proceed.

Suggested procurement-friendly amendment (one paragraph):
"Redwood will not bill model compute for prompt prefixes that are served entirely from Redwood’s prefix/KV cache (exact token-for-token matches). For partial matches, Redwood will bill model compute only for the tokens that require model execution. Prefetch/warm-up calls are treated as API requests and billable; however, Customer and Redwood may agree to a Prefetch Credit in the SOW to offset a negotiated portion of prefetch volume. Redwood will provide per-request accounting (total tokens, cache-served tokens, computed tokens) as part of the invoice appendix to enable audit and reconciliation."

Session affinity and metadata handling (short bullets):
- Match keys: cache matching is content-first (hashed prompt content + model version). Session IDs are not required for a match; they are only used when customers request session-scoped isolation.
- Metadata differences: small per-request metadata that modifies the token stream will break an exact-match; we treat exact-match on the tokenized sequence. For typical cases where metadata is passed separately (e.g., headers), we recommend using Redwood’s separate metadata fields (non-tokenized) so they don’t affect cache matching.

Next steps:
- If Orchid prefers Option B (enterprise addendum) we will ship a draft SOW with exact rebate numbers (Ben’s proposal above) and a sample invoice appendix.
- If you want to see a proforma with your traffic, send estimated monthly tokens and an expected reuse rate and we’ll model costs for both options.
